svg.title: Summarization: where it is configured, why it must be paired with a null0 route, and what it costs
svg.desc: A topology shows two areas, each with an ABR, the ABR summarising one area block into the backbone and the other ABR receiving the summary. Three rules are given: summarise at the boundary that owns the detail, meaning the ABR for inter-area prefixes and the ASBR for external ones; make the summary the longest match for nothing, because detail always wins over summary; and pair it with a null0 route so that dropped traffic is dropped visibly. A second panel explains the null0 logic in three states: all member prefixes up, so the summary is advertised and traffic follows detail; one member down, so the summary stays up and the traffic is silently discarded inside the area; and every member down, so the null0 keeps the summary alive and the traffic is dropped at the boundary where the fault actually is. A right panel lists the five costs of summarization: loss of visibility, loss of traffic engineering granularity, summary flaps move more traffic, aggregation errors become network-wide, and troubleshooting shifts inside the area.
svg.text: Summarization is a trade of visibility for scale, and the trade is only safe with a null0
A summary without null0 is a design flaw: it promises reachability the network cannot deliver
WHERE IT IS CONFIGURED
Backbone (area 0)
ABR-1 · area 10 range
ABR-2 · area 20 range
one summary each way
10.10.0.0/16 block, owned here
200 /24s → 1 prefix
Summarise at the boundary that owns the detail: ABR for
inter-area, ASBR for external. Never summarise in the middle.
The three rules
1. A summary must never be the longest match for anything.
2. Detail always wins — that is what makes it safe.
3. Pair every summary with null0, so what cannot be
delivered is dropped at the boundary, not inside an area.
Without null0, the summary lives on a null route nobody owns.
WHAT null0 CHANGES, IN THREE STATES
All members up
Summary advertised, detail exists,
traffic follows the detail entries.
The null0 is never used — it is a
statement of intent, not a path.
One member down, no null0
The summary stays up as long as any
member survives. Traffic still enters
and is dropped deep inside the area.
The fault is invisible from the core.
Same state, with null0
Traffic for the dead /24 hits the
boundary and is dropped there, where
the counters prove it is that prefix.
Same outage, but now it is diagnosable.
FIVE COSTS OF SUMMARIZATION — LIST THEM IN THE DESIGN DOCUMENT OR DO NOT CONFIGURE IT
1. Visibility: the core no longer knows whether a specific /24 exists — “show ip route” on a core router answers a smaller question than you think.
2. Granularity: you cannot traffic-engineer an individual prefix, only the whole block. Per-site policy needs detail at the policy point.
3. Blast radius: a summary flap moves all member traffic, where a detail flap moved one subnet.
4. Aggregation error: a wrong mask or an overlap becomes a network-wide black hole instead of a local one.
5. Troubleshooting shifts inside the area: the person with the ticket sees a core that says the destination is reachable, because at the summary level it is.
